sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text: Piezoelectric energy harvesting (PEH) provides an essential mode for the transformation of mechanical vibration to electrical form for providing continuous power to wireless sensor nodes in today’s connected world. This work describes an analytical model based on the Euler-Bernoulli model. The proposed model is in agreement with the FEM simulation model, with results differing by $6 \%$ . Variation in geometric parameter, the effect of resonant frequency, output power and stability of the design provides a constraint domain for structure optimization have been described along with the effect of damping. The designed harvester generates a power of $1 . 3 1 \mathrm { m W }$ at $9 0 \mathsf { H z }$ resonant frequency.

sections.heading: KEYWORDS
sections.text: Piezoelectric energy harvesting; bimorph; cantilever optimization electromechanical conversion; mechanical damping; electrical damping

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Piezoelectric energy harvesting can generate adequate power at micro-scales to power wireless sensor nodes and micro-scale devices. Due to the capability of piezoelectric harvesters to convert applied mechanical strain into usable electric energy, they have been a major area of research over the last decade. The performance of piezoelectric energy harvester (PEH) depends on a piezoelectric material, poling, stress direction and resonant frequency. Euler-Bernoulli theorem [1] has been used to determine the resonance frequency of the cantilever design, which is mostly used as a mechanical structure to design the harvester.

The resonant frequency is a very essential parameter to design a PEH as a peak power response is achieved at the resonant frequency. It is essential to model the resonant frequency to match the ambient vibration frequency of the source for which the harvester is being designed. Many mechanical design modifications, like the addition of proof mass to increase the strain, which increases the power as well as reduces the resonant frequency, have been utilized in the literature [2–8]. Mechanical structure and shape of the device also play an important role in determining the resonant frequency and output power. Many researchers have proposed complex non-linear structures [9–11] to improve device performance. Cantilever structure extracts an adequate power output. The present work models a PEH as a cantilever structure in both analytical and simulative perspective. Simulation is based on finite element analysis while the analytical model is based on Euler-Bernoulli theorem has been studied in this work. Structure Damping is another important parameter for a PEH. This system suffers from two kinds of damping, i.e. mechanical and electrical damping. The work proposes models to analyze both types of damping and their effect on PEH outputs.

sections.heading: 2. Modeling of a Cantilever Structure
sections.text: Modeling of the cantilever as a PEH is essential to analyze the effects of geometric parameters on the harvester. PEH system has two parts mechanical and electrical. Mechanical modeling determines the tip displacement and the resonant frequency of the cantilever structure.

sections.heading: 3. Optimization of Cantilever Structure for Capturing Ambient Vibrations
sections.text:
Design parameter play an important role in determining the two governing output for the harvester, i.e. resonant frequency and output power, as shown in Eqs. (5) and (22). The safety factor is essential in defining the stability of the system as described by Eq. (23). Length of the beam and proof mass are the first parameter to be optimized. The parameter of the harvester has been described in Table 1. The list contains the parameter, which is already set due to the constraints while it also enlists the parameter that is needed to be optimized to attain an effective piezoelectric energy harvester. A variation in both parameters is carried out in order to see their effect on output parameters. As the length of the beam and proof mass increase, resonant frequency tends to decrease. To achieve the target resonant frequency, the length parameter needs to be maintained in the third segment as described in Figure 4. A variation in length parameters is carried out, which, indicates their dependence on resonant frequency and safety factor. A longer beam and proof mass length will lead to a decrease in the safety factor and an increase in mechanical damping of the device. Hence, among the length parameters capable of producing the targeted resonant frequency at $9 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , an appropriate beam length and proof mass length is to be determined. A comparison of volume, safety factor, resonant frequency and stress on the device is shown in Figure 5. All the design have the first resonant frequency around $9 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Design 6 is the safest design, while it also has the lowest volume. Among the designs Design 2 having $L = 2 1 \mathrm { m m }$ and $\mathrm { l } _ { \mathrm { m } } { = } 8 \mathrm { m m }$ gives the maximum stress; hence, is considered the optimized structure for length parameter study. The thickness of piezoelectric and substrate are to be optimized—both these parameter effect resonant frequency and power density of the design. A variation in thickness is carried out. The thicker the layers have better power density as the amount of accumulated charges on the layer will be high. However, as the layer becomes thicker the resonant frequency tends to decrease. These variations are shown in Figure 6. Hence, a thinner layer is desired to maintain the resonant frequency and an appropriate power density. sections.heading: 3.1. Electromechanical Conversion
sections.text:
Mechanical to electrical conversion is a significant part of the piezoelectric energy harvesting process. Higher the amount of stress the piezoelectric layer experiences, higher is the power generated by the piezoelectric layer.

![](images/e22f8f12f06e7301b7f6fb8d2deb119e0a6d293f565cb20c821d4ec84b483e21.jpg)  
Stress and Output generated power vs frequency.

![](images/f2ceb13b846f1eb2679ff543e0e39d240431bc3bd7c40a7165c02787946ac3e8.jpg)  
Total displacement and Electric potential vs frequency.

Electromechanical coupling displays the conversion of stress on the piezo layer and equal conversion of electrical power by those layers [13, 15]. More is the stress, larger is the displacement of the device, which increases the quantity of accumulated charges, and higher is the potential developed on the layer. A variation of stress and generated output power with frequency variation has been shown in Figure 7. An efficient mechanical to electrical conversion takes place, as the point of peak stress is similar to the point of peak-generated power. It can be concluded that a peak stress of around $8 . 2 \mathrm { M N } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ results in a $0 . 4 5 \mathrm { m W }$ of power. These deformation cause accumulation of charges on the surface of the layer. Accumulation of charge leads to an electric field being developed which cause a potential difference between the two layers. The relationship between total displacements to the electric potential is shown in Figure 8.

sections.heading: 4. Damping Effects
sections.text: Damping is an essential part of analyzing the PEH. Damping helps in calculating the losses suffered by the system both in mechanical as well as electrical domain.

sections.heading: 4.1. Mechanical Damping
sections.text:
Mechanical damping is comprised of flapping air, internal friction, beam support losses and squeeze air film damping. Mechanical damping mostly depends on air damping and internal friction [7,8].

sections.heading: 5. Discussion
sections.text: The piezoelectric bimorph harvester is capable of producing $0 . 5 \mathrm { m W }$ of power at $9 . 8 \mathrm { m } /$ $s ^ { 2 }$ acceleration across a $4 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ resistor. The device is compared with previously existing devices based on a piezoelectric material, device volume, resonant frequency, load resistance and power density (Table 3). The device simulated here has a lesser volume with an appropriate resonance frequency for ambient vibration sources $( { < } 1 0 0 \mathrm { H z } )$ and an acceleration of $9 . 8 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ . The output power density for the device is better than those in the literature using the same piezoelectric material, i.e. Zinc Oxide. For a similar load resistance, i.e. $4 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ the device gives a comparable power density at lower operating frequency.

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: An Euler-Bernoulli based analytical model for PEH has been described in this work. Geometric parameter affects the resonant frequency, output power and stability of the system has been utilized in order to optimize the structure to extract ambient vibration precisely. The resonant frequency decreases with an increase in length and decrease in thickness of layers of the cantilever structure. Power density also increases with increment in length and decrement in the thickness of layers. Therefore, it is essential to have thin film and longer devices, which could provide better performance keeping in mind the volume constraint $( < 1 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } )$ . Optimization of the device has helped in determining the length of the beam as $2 1 \mathrm { m m }$ and length of proof mass as $8 \mathrm { m m }$ for achieving the target resonant frequency of $9 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . The thickness of layers is maintained at $0 . 0 6 \mathrm { m m }$ for piezoelectric layer and $0 . 0 4 \mathrm { m m }$ for the substrate layer for providing optimum output. The electromechanical analysis depicts an efficient conversion of mechanical stress to output power as well as displacement to an electric voltage. Damping in PEH is a combination of both mechanical and electrical. The value of mechanical damping parameter in the simulation and analytical model is around 0.048. Mechanical damping coefficient restricts the width of the device as well as the thickness of proof mass to a minimum. At the optimum condition of resonant frequency, the mechanical damping coefficient becomes equal to the electrical damping coefficient. The piezoelectric bimorph energy harvester can generate $1 . 3 1 \mathrm { m W }$ of peak power at $\mathbf { \dot { \omega } } _ { 1 \mathbf { g } } ^ { * }$ acceleration at a resonant frequency of $9 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . The work establishes a basis for further optimization of design to improve the performance of the system in terms of both resonant frequency and output power for various other applications.
